# Pipeup: functional specification

**Status:** Generated from the workspace · 9 designed journeys · **Last updated:** 2026-11-10

Fingerprints: source 458704cb · prototype e2b6658a, up to date · proofs 2026-11-10.

This file is written by `npm run build` and never edited by hand. Change the brief (`project.md`), a step's `## Requirements` and `## Acceptance criteria`, `data/` or `docs/changes.md`, then run `npm run build`. The workspace's ids are listed in the appendix.

It holds everything in one file. The same content comes in parts: an overview and a part per journey for people (`docs/spec/`), and the contract, the requirements as data and the checklist for the team that builds it (`docs/build/`).

## Purpose
Pipe up, right where the work is.

### Problem
People share work as standalone HTML files: reports, specs, prototypes and slide decks, many of them written by AI agents. Those files have no good way to collect feedback. Reviewers reply in chat threads that lose the context of what they were looking at, and the author (or the agent working for them) has to guess where each remark belongs.

### Value
Pipeup turns any HTML page into a reviewable document with one script tag. Reviewers select words, click a block or drop a pin and comment in place. Comments stay in their own browser, and Copy comments as Markdown turns them into text that says exactly where each comment is, ready to send to the author or paste into an AI agent.

## The brief
### What sets it apart
- No accounts and no servers: Pipeup itself never sends anything anywhere, and a page opened from disk works.
- The page stays the author's: nothing is restyled, moved or covered, and outside comment mode the page behaves exactly as before.
- Comments carry their place: the slide or section, the element, the quoted words or the pin, so an agent knows where to act.
- One set of gestures covers text, blocks, pins and the page as a whole.

## Platform

Every step meets these.

- **Runs on:** current desktop and mobile browsers, on any HTML page opened from disk, served locally or hosted on the web.
- **Appearance:** the light theme by default; the person can switch to dark or automatic from the comment control's menu, and the choice is remembered for that page in that browser.
- **Sizes:** phones from 390 px wide upward; on wide windows the comment column sits beside the content, and on narrow screens threads open below what they are about and All comments takes the full width.
- **Input:** pointer, keyboard (Shift+Alt+C, ⇧⌥C on a Mac, toggles comment mode; Esc steps out) and touch.
- **Start and stop:** the page opens with its comments showing and comment mode off; comments, the person's name and the hidden choice are kept in that browser for that page.

## Users
- **Maya Lindqvist**, Reviewer; reads a colleague's HTML report or deck and says what she thinks: someone sent them an HTML file; they want to say what they think about a sentence, a block or a spot, and hand it back, with no account to make. Goal: Say what she thinks about a sentence, a block or a spot on the page, and hand it back without making an account.
- **Tom Adeyemi**, Author; writes reports and decks as HTML, often with a coding agent, and asks people to review them: they made the page (or an agent did), add one line to it, and want every comment pinned to the exact place so an agent can act on it. Goal: Collect every reviewer's comments pinned to the exact place, and hand them to an agent that acts on them.

## Open questions
2 questions are open. Each one says where it is asked; answer it there. The full list, with what each holds up: `docs/open-questions.md`.

- How will this be observed: moderated sessions, or something counted? _(Brief)_
- How many pastes, and who judges that the agent found the place? _(Brief)_

## Data and behaviour
- No data yet: entities, who may do what and sample rows are optional (`data/`).
## Success criteria
- **SC-001** A reviewer with no account comments on a sentence within a minute of opening the page. Measure: **Open question:** How will this be observed: moderated sessions, or something counted?
- **SC-002** An author pastes copied comments into a coding agent and the agent finds every place without asking. Measure: **Open question:** How many pastes, and who judges that the agent found the place?

## Out of scope
- Reviewing images or PDFs on their own.
- A hosted service, accounts, dashboards or notifications: sharing and live review are optional add-ons the author chooses.
- Rich comments: formatting, images or embedded content. Comments are plain text with line breaks and links.
- Replacing the chat or tracker where decisions are made; Pipeup collects the feedback and hands it on.

## For the team that builds it

Build Pipeup on the stack you choose. This specification says what it must do and how to check it; the design workspace beside it says how it looks and behaves. Read them in this order.

1. **The contract:** the functional requirements and their acceptance criteria (what to validate), the success criteria and what is out of scope, below.
2. **The screens:** each step below names its screen's files: its guidance (`journeys/<journey>/screens/<step>.md`: purpose, content, interactions and states) and its mock (`<step>.html`, built from the design system). Each journey's steps and flow are in `journeys/<journey>/journey.md`.
3. **The design system:** the tokens in `design-system/foundations/<foundation>/foundation.css`, with when to use each in `foundation.md` (Color, Density, Icons, Layout, Motion, Navigation, Philosophy, Radius, Typography); the components in `design-system/components/<basic|composite>/<component>/component.md` (when to use, variants, anatomy, accessibility, interaction), each shown in `specimen.html`. Every value in every theme and preset is in `docs/tokens.json`, in plain units (colours in sRGB, sizes in points, durations in milliseconds, easing as curves) and in the W3C design-tokens format: take every colour, size and timing from it, never from the mocks' CSS. The screens use: Avatar (`design-system/components/basic/cmp-avatar/component.md`), Button (`design-system/components/basic/cmp-button/component.md`), Chip (`design-system/components/basic/cmp-chip/component.md`), Code block (`design-system/components/basic/cmp-code-block/component.md`, with its Contract), Comment card (`design-system/components/composite/cmp-comment-card/component.md`), Comment control (`design-system/components/basic/cmp-comment-control/component.md`), Comments panel (`design-system/components/composite/cmp-comments-panel/component.md`), Dialog (`design-system/components/basic/cmp-dialog/component.md`, with its Contract), Highlight (`design-system/components/basic/cmp-highlight/component.md`), Icon button (`design-system/components/basic/cmp-icon-button/component.md`), Inline alert (`design-system/components/basic/cmp-inline-alert/component.md`), Key (`design-system/components/basic/cmp-kbd/component.md`), Naming bar (`design-system/components/composite/cmp-naming-bar/component.md`), Pin (`design-system/components/basic/cmp-pin/component.md`), Popover menu (`design-system/components/composite/cmp-popover-menu/component.md`, with its Contract), Prompt card (`design-system/components/composite/cmp-prompt-card/component.md`, with its Contract), Slide (`design-system/components/basic/cmp-slide/component.md`), Switch (`design-system/components/basic/cmp-switch/component.md`), Text field (`design-system/components/basic/cmp-text-field/component.md`). A component's Contract describes its behaviour in terms any platform builds the same way (parts, states, inputs, events, geometry with units and axes, and looks); on a platform other than the web, build it from the Contract, not from the markup.
4. **The reference pictures:** `docs/references/` holds a picture of every screen state and every component variant and state, as the design renders it (light and dark). They define what "looks as designed" means: compare your screens with them, state by state. A picture's frame is the screen's content only: whatever your platform's window adds (a title bar, a toolbar) is outside it. Beside each picture, a `.json` file of the same name holds its layout as data: the frame's size, and for each named element (a screen's parts, a component's reference points) its position and size in points and its text and background colours. Check your screens against them automatically, without looking at pictures; for a component whose view changes (a camera, a zoom, a turn), its points at the default view and at each end of each range say where your build must draw them.
5. **The stand-ins:** the mocks cannot draw some parts as the product looks on its platform (a 3D model, a material and its light, a video, a sound, a platform's own control). Where a mock shows one, it shows only a stand-in (its place, size, colour and state), and so do its reference pictures: never copy a stand-in, and never take its picture as the look; build the look from where each line says it is defined.
   - Review a document: Drop a pin on an exact spot (screen; its pictures `docs/references/screens/jny-review-a-document/drop-a-pin--*` show the stand-in):
     - The pin: the mock shows the mock draws it in its own row under "The path", in flow. Look: in the product the pin's point sits at the exact spot Maya Option-clicked, kept as a fraction of the width and height of the element it is on (here the heading's row), so it stays put when the window is resized; cmp-pin's page says how it looks.
   - Review a slide deck: Drop a pin on a slide (screen; its pictures `docs/references/screens/jny-review-a-slide-deck/pin-on-a-slide--*` show the stand-in):
     - The pin: the mock shows the mock draws it at the slide's top-right corner, on the slide's pin layer. Look: in the product its point is at the exact spot Maya Option-clicked, kept as a fraction of the slide's width and height, so it keeps its place when the slide is resized (cmp-pin).
   - Review on a phone: Tap a block and type (screen; its pictures `docs/references/screens/jny-review-on-a-phone/tap-to-comment--*` show the stand-in):
     - The on-screen keyboard: the mock shows the mock cannot draw it; the box sits below the paragraph as it would above the keyboard. Look: the box and its buttons stay in the part of the screen the keyboard leaves, below what the comment is about when it fits, above it otherwise.
6. **The icons and assets:** artwork the product draws as it is, never redrawn or replaced: the design's own icons, drawn from `design-system/foundations/fdn-icons/outline.svg` and `design-system/foundations/fdn-icons/solid.svg` (one set per icon preset; each step below lists the icons its screen shows, and each component its own). An icon or asset from anywhere else (another icon set, a system symbol, a placeholder) is a defect under Only what is designed.
7. **The reference prototype:** `prototype/` and its proofs (`prototype/proofs.json`, the last run in `prototype/proofs/report.json`) show the requirements can be met. It is a reference, not the product to ship, and not a choice of how to build it.

When they disagree, the requirements and acceptance criteria win, then a screen's guidance, then its mock; the prototype never overrides them.

Which source is the truth for what:

- **Behaviour:** the requirements and acceptance criteria; each criterion's "Set up" says how to reach its Given.
- **A component's behaviour and geometry:** its Contract (parts, states, inputs, events, geometry, looks, the names that cross to other components, who holds the focus, and how a view changes).
- **Text:** the mocks, as they are written, and each screen's Wording for text that depends on the data.
- **Every value** (colour, size, timing): `docs/tokens.json`.
- **Looks:** the reference pictures in `docs/references/` and the layout beside each; for a part a mock shows only as a stand-in, where its stand-in line says the look is defined, never the picture.
- **Artwork:** the icon sets and the assets.

No fact you need is only in a mock's code or in the prototype. If you find one there, it is a gap in this design: say so in your feedback (below), and do not take it from the code.

### Done means

It is done when you can show it, not when you say so. Deliver this evidence, in this order:

1. **A working slice first:** the first journey, Add Pipeup to a page, from launch to its end, by pointer and by keyboard, on the real platform, shown in pictures before any other journey is built.
2. **Every acceptance criterion as an automated check** named after its id. The run's report lists every id as passed or failed, and counts 74, as many as this specification; a run that counts fewer is not done.
3. **Every screen state beside its reference picture:** a picture of each state the screens design, set beside its picture in `docs/references/screens/`, in each appearance the Platform names.
4. **Every journey played** from start to end, by pointer and by keyboard.
5. **The success criteria measured**, as each one says.

Return the evidence in one folder, with your feedback on the design (below): the Validation checklist at the end of this specification filled in, one piece of evidence per line, as `checklist.md` (keep its Version column as it is: it says which version of each item you built); the report of the automated checks as `report.xml` (JUnit), `report.json` (each id with `passed` or `failed`) or `report.txt` (one line per id with passed or failed); and your pictures in `pictures/`, each named as its reference picture is (`pictures/<journey>/<step>--<state>--<frame>--<theme>.png`).

### Your feedback on the design

Tell us where this design failed you, so the next build gets it right the first time. Never change the design yourself: build it as designed, or ask when the work depends on it.

- **As you go, `feedback.md`:** one line each time the design did not say, two parts of the design disagree, it cannot be built as designed on the platform, a state, asset or text is missing or it works as designed but feels wrong: `- <gap|conflict|infeasible|missing|friction> · <the design item: a requirement, criterion, screen, component, token, asset or picture>: <what happened>. Did: <what you did>. Propose: <the change to the design>`.
- **At each checkpoint** (the working slice, each journey, done), `retrospective.md`, with three parts, each a list of `- <the design item>: <what happened>. Cost: <the work redone, or the choice that would have been different>. Prevent: <the fact that would have prevented it, written as a requirement, not a technology>`: `## Left out or unclear` (what the design left out or said so it could be read two ways), `## Stated but missed` (what the design stated but you missed, and what would have made it hard to miss), `## Our own mistakes` (your own mistakes, which do not change the design).

Return both with your evidence. The owner accepts, rejects or defers each item; an accepted one changes the design, and the next reply says what changed.

### Only what is designed

Build only what the requirements, the screens and the components design. A control, screen, text or behaviour that is not designed is a defect, not an improvement. When something seems missing, write it down as a question with a proposed answer and ask; the work that depends on it waits.

Before building a step, read its guidance and its mock (each frame's mock when it has several), the Contracts of the components it lists, its Wording and stand-ins, its icons and assets, and its reference pictures and their layouts. Each criterion's Set up says how to reach its Given; a criterion with none starts on its step's screen.
